results.title: Choice of priors — Uncertainty Quantification
results.content: # Choice of priors. # Choice of priors#. In contrast, in the case of studies with a small amount of data, the prior choice has a significant impact on the posterior, and thus one has to be careful when choosing it. In Bayesian methodology, we differentiate between two types of priors: informative priors and non-informative priors. As the names suggest, the informative prior reflects a clear prior knowledge of the parameter \(\theta\), while the non-informative prior reflects a very small to complete lack of prior knowledge. Priors, in general, incorporate the amount of information we have about the model of the parameters before seeing the data. When researchers can specify a particular prior distribution favouring a range of values for the parameter over others, we say that they set an *informative prior*. The choice of a suitable informative prior can depend on several considerations, such as the findings of other similar studies (e.g. meta-analysis) or expert opinions. When in particular the distributions of the posterior \(\pi(\theta|x\_1,\dots,x\_n)\) is of the same family as the prior distribution for the likelihood of the data, we say that the prior is a conjugate prior with respect to the likelihood. * Beta distribution is a conjugate prior with respect to a Bernoulli likelihood. * Gamma distribution is a conjugate prior with respect to a Poisson likelihood. If prior information about \(\theta\) is missing, alternative priors can be considered. Those latter are called non-informative priors. The first prior that comes to mind is the uniform prior (or flat prior), which gives the same likelihood to each possible value of the parameter \(\theta\). Under a reparameterization of \(\theta\), the prior on the new parameter still should reflect the no information property, but this is not the case. This is contradictory, as \(\phi\) has no longer a non-informative prior. Though it is known to be a non-informative prior in literature, it is not entirely non-informative. Therefore this prior reflects information directly from the sampling distribution, and it is defined by. Lastly, we can mention another type of non-informative prior called the reference prior, and it maximizes the missing information in the experiment [Robert and others, 2007]. For more details about the choice and types of non-informative priors see [Bernardo, 1997].

results.title: Keyword Cannibalization - What It Is and How to Resolve It | 97th Floor
results.content: Keyword cannibalization occurs when multiple pages on a website compete for the same or similar keywords. Keyword cannibalization refers to a situation where multiple pages on a single website inadvertently compete against each other for the same or similar keywords. Imagine a scenario where a website has several articles or pages targeting the keyword "best digital marketing strategies." Instead of reinforcing each other, these pages clash, vying for attention from search engines like Google. Understanding the intricacies of keyword cannibalization can help you find the right balance in content creation and keyword targeting to ensure that each page on your website serves a unique and distinct purpose in your overall SEO strategy. With keyword cannibalization, the value of inbound links is dispersed across several pages instead of consolidating on one. When they detect multiple pages from the same site competing for a keyword, it can lead to devaluation in rankings. If a site has numerous pages competing for the same keywords, search engines waste resources crawling and indexing similar content. Detecting keyword cannibalization involves identifying which pages are competing against each other for the same keywords. If you notice fluctuations or several pages ranking for the same term at different times, it could indicate keyword cannibalization. * Identifying Pages Ranking for Unintended Keywords: Sometimes, a page may rank for keywords that it wasn’t specifically targeted for, indicating potential cannibalization. This process involves making strategic decisions about your website’s content and structure to ensure that each page serves a unique purpose and targets distinct keywords. Additionally, it's important to audit all internal links on the site to confirm that any links containing the anchor text for the cannibalizing keyword are directed to the focus page. By adhering to these practices, you can effectively prevent keyword cannibalization, ensuring that your website's content strategy remains robust and your SEO efforts are not undermined. Understanding these aspects of keyword cannibalization can help in developing more effective SEO strategies and in maintaining the health and competitiveness of your website. For businesses with multiple locations, keyword cannibalization can lead to confusion in local search results, where the wrong location page ranks for location-specific searches.

results.title: Keyword Cannibalization: What It (Really) Is & How to Fix It
results.content: Keyword cannibalization is an SEO issue that happens when multiple pages on a website target the same or similar keywords. But it’s crucial to remember that you only have a real cannibalization issue when multiple pages target the same keyword and hurt a site’s organic performance. You could argue that this is textbook keyword cannibalization because one page is seemingly “cannibalizing” traffic to the other page. The trick to finding real cannibalization issues is to look for pages that target the same keywords *and* fulfill the same or very similar intent. Moz may very well have a keyword cannibalization issue here, but not all of these pages are problematic. Check for multiple ranking URLs. If Google ranks multiple URLs for a keyword, that can be a sign of a cannibalization issue. For example, removing all internal links with the cannibalizing keyword as the anchor is likely to affect the page’s rankings for other keywords too. The same is true for removing mentions of the cannibalizing keyword from the page.

results.title: How to Check Keyword Cannibalization with Ahrefs (and Fix It)
results.content: # How to Check Keyword Cannibalization with Ahrefs (and Fix It) Keyword cannibalization is a common issue that many website owners and content creators face. It occurs when multiple pages on your site compete for the same keyword or closely related terms, ultimately hurting your SEO performance. Thankfully, tools like Ahrefs can help you identify and resolve keyword cannibalization effectively. ## What is Keyword Cannibalization? Keyword cannibalization happens when more than one page on your website targets the same keyword. Search engines, like Google, get confused about which page to rank for that specific keyword, resulting in lower overall rankings. Common Causes of Keyword Cannibalization: – Multiple blog posts targeting the same topic. – Product pages optimized for similar keywords. ## How to Identify Keyword Cannibalization Using Ahrefs Ahrefs is one of the most powerful SEO tools available, and it offers a simple method for detecting keyword cannibalization. 2. Use the filter option to find keywords for which multiple URLs are ranking. – Apply a Keyword filter to search for specific keywords you suspect might be cannibalized. Ahrefs will display all URLs that rank for each keyword, making it easy to spot overlapping pages. ### Step 4: Analyze Content Once you’ve identified potential cannibalization issues, open each page and evaluate: – Content Quality: Are both pages providing value, or are they redundant? Use internal links to guide search engines and users to the most authoritative page for a specific keyword. Ensure that the anchor text reflects the targeted keyword, boosting the preferred page’s relevance. Ensure that each page targets a unique keyword or variation. Conduct thorough keyword research and map out which pages should target which keywords. If older pages are cannibalizing newer ones, consider updating or repurposing the content to target different keywords. Implement a solid content strategy to prevent future cannibalization by planning keyword targets and user intent before creating new pages. Keyword cannibalization can undermine your SEO efforts, but with tools like Ahrefs, identifying and fixing these issues becomes manageable. By consolidating content, optimizing internal links, and differentiating keyword targets, you can enhance your website’s performance and ensure that your pages are working together, not against each other.
